source.title: A Large Scale Investigation of Scaling Limits in Chemical Language Models
source.authors: Roshan Balaji; Kamran Chitsaz; Quentin Fournier; N. Bhatt; S. Chandar

record.tranche_reason: Tests SAE feature accessibility in chemical language models using property associations and functional-group probes, rather than testing toy-model superposition geometry or feature competition.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports linear-probe results for chemical properties and validity, but those do not measure feature overlap, capacity competition, or SAE recovery and are not included as rows. The SAE results below are the claim-relevant measurements and comparisons.
record.test_reason: The SAE analysis in chemical language models gives its own results on whether a dictionary recovers sparse, property-aligned features and whether SAE latents expose functional groups better than residual neurons. That bears on V4 in a new domain (molecular transformers). It is ancillary to a scaling study, so the test is weak and indirect, not the T2 the reader assigned.
record.authors_conclusion: The paper's main conclusion is that pretraining loss and internal representations keep improving with scale while goal-directed generation saturates near 5M parameters. On the SAE part, the record's paraphrase is broadly right. Feature–property associations strengthen with training and scale. SAE latents beat neuron probes for 7 of 10 groups by up to 0.04 F1, which the authors call a modest but consistent gain. They say the association measures reflect alignment with properties, not single-concept encoding.
record.recipe_differences: Uses layer-wise linear probes and BatchTopK SAEs on chemical language models; it does not reproduce the original toy-network feature-superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE monosemanticity trajectories differ by layer: the early-layer value rises, while middle and late layers peak mid-training and decline slightly.
record.code_released: not stated; the paper says it will release code and checkpoints but gives no URL
record.problems: The SAE feature-recovery evidence is from one 32M reference model and one middle layer for the functional-group comparison. The F1 table reports averages over folds without uncertainty estimates. The reported feature-property measurements do not establish that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.

untested.parts: All of it: toy models, feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions.
All of it: no capacity or feature-importance analysis.
All of it: no study of the causes of polysemanticity.
Whether features are spread across many individual neurons. The neuron baseline is a whole-residual linear probe, so per-neuron polysemanticity is not measured.
Completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, and canonicality of SAE features.

missing.what: SAE monosemanticity rising with compute and model size across 0.5M–1B models (about 0.15 to 0.35+)
SAE reconstruction quality: fraction of variance explained rises quickly and saturates near or above 0.9 (32M BPE, layer 6)

record.verdict_notes: The SAE work is a secondary probe inside a scaling study. The 'neurons' baseline is a linear probe on the whole residual stream, not individual neurons, so it does not test neuron polysemanticity. Higher SAE-latent F1 may partly reflect the 16x wider, nonlinear basis. There are no uncertainty estimates for the F1 values. The record's limits_scope label for r12–r14 is kept, but those rows should be absent, not observed. The tranche is corrected from T2 to T3 (new domain).

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by limited capacity or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises for other reasons and whether it is evidence of superposition.
The study tests SAE feature-property associations and functional-group recovery in chemical language models, but not whether real general-purpose LLM features are spread across neurons.
Completeness, stability across settings or training runs, and canonicality of SAE features are not measured.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional subspaces.

relationships.condition: 32M PubChem-SMILES model, middle layer, 7 of 10 functional groups
relationships.reason: Probes on SAE latents beat residual-neuron probes by 0.013–0.034 F1 (r5–r11), so the SAE dictionary recovers functional-group features at least as accessibly.
relationships.display_finding: Probes on SAE latents beat probes on residual neurons by 0.013–0.034 F1, so the dictionary exposed functional-group features at least as accessibly as neurons.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: 32M PubChem-SMILES model, middle layer, 7 of 10 functional groups
source_check.reason: Table D2 confirms r5–r11: SAE probe F1 is 0.986–0.999, exceeding residual-stream probes by 0.013–0.034; this supports chemical-feature accessibility in a sparse dictionary.

relationships.condition: Benzene, aromatic N, tertiary amine, and SAE property-association measures
relationships.reason: No SAE advantage for three groups (r12–r14). Only 21% of features are property-associated and mean max correlation is 0.33 (r1, r4). The authors call the gain modest, not decisive.
relationships.display_finding: The SAE gave no advantage for benzene, aromatic nitrogen and tertiary amine groups. Only 21% of features were associated with a property, the mean maximum correlation was 0.33, and the authors call the gain modest rather than decisive.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Benzene, aromatic N, tertiary amine, and SAE property-association measures
source_check.reason: R12–r14 still show high SAE feature accessibility, and r1/r4 show positive property associations. V4 requires neither superiority over residual-stream probes nor alignment of every dictionary feature with the 36 evaluated properties. These results qualify stronger interpretability claims, not V4 as written.

relation.reason: The study measures dictionary feature–property associations and functional-group accessibility, providing its own indirect evidence relevant to V4.

tranche.reason: Chemical language models provide a new setting with original measurements of sparse dictionary features and their chemical-property associations.

source_check.notes: The source is arXiv v3 dated 1 October 2026. Table D2 compares multivariate probes, not individual neurons; the synthesis statement is factually correct for this study, but lack of SAE superiority does not itself limit V4.
